title: Caste, honestly
hookLine: the Gurus rejected caste, yet caste divisions still show in some Sikh places

cards: In the langar hall, everyone sits on the floor in the same row: the farmer next to the doctor, the cleaner next to the landlord. That row is a sermon without words.
In some villages in Punjab, you may find two gurdwaras within walking distance of each other. Same Guru, same hymns. Different families, divided by caste.
A row on the floor says one thing; two buildings say another. Today is about the gap between them.

teach.b: First, what the Gurus said. At Ang 349 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says to recognize the divine light in everyone and not to ask about caste, because in the world beyond there is no caste.
At Ang 15 he says he stands with the lowest of the low, and has nothing to do with the great. Guru Amar Das, at Ang 1127, warns: let no one be proud of caste.
The Guru Granth Sahib itself holds hymns by bhagats from castes others looked down on, set beside the Gurus' own words.

teach.h: ONE ROW, ONE FLOOR, ONE BOWL.
teach.b: Second, what the Gurus did: langar and sangat, everyone in one row on one floor, and the Khalsa, where, tradition says, those who first came forward were from different castes and drank amrit from one bowl.
Third, the honest part. Caste did not disappear.

teach.h: CASTE STILL SHOWS IN SOME PLACES.
teach.b: In some places it still shows: in separate gurdwaras, in marriages arranged within a caste, in surnames that carry old ranks, and in Sikhs from castes once called low who say they are still made to feel it.
Sikh writers, reformers and Dalit Sikhs have called this out, using the Gurus' own words. And not only in villages: some diaspora towns have gurdwaras founded along caste lines too.
When violence over a marriage across caste makes the news, Sikhs answer in two ways. Some say it's Punjabi culture, not Sikhi. Others say that it's a Sikh problem, whether anyone likes it or not.
Both point to the same Gurus. And if anyone is in danger over a marriage, local emergency help comes first. Fourth, the line.

teach.h: THE STANDARD IS NOT IN DOUBT.
teach.b: A path isn't judged only by how well its followers keep it; it also gives them a standard.
On caste, that standard is not in doubt.

how: In gurdwaras, all eat together in langar sitting in one row, and the Rehat Maryada rejects caste distinctions; in some places caste still shapes marriages and gurdwara membership, and Sikh reformers work against it.

games.q: you arrive at langar and the only open space in the row is beside someone your family was raised to keep apart from. what does the langar row ask?
games.why: langar seats everyone in one row on one floor; the Gurus built it that way on purpose.

practice: People get sorted by accent, job, family name; gently ask whether you sort anyone without meaning to, and look at it plainly, without punishing yourself.
Then picture yourself in the langar row beside the very person that bias would put elsewhere, and stay a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Caste. A ranking of people by birth, rejected by the Gurus in word and practice, and still showing in some Sikh places. Today's word.

orig.note: jaat, caste or birth-group; the word the Gurus tell Sikhs not to ask about at Ang 349.

carryVoice: Your line: the gurus rejected it. The work is in the gap between the hymn and the village. I'll be here tomorrow.
